Day 22 checkpoint: Before running more trials, I must test the leading hypothesis (p=0.51) that a ~6-day environmental cycle is phase-shifting all four instruments. This is the critical fork; running more trials without this check is scientifically inefficient.

Day 22 showed coordinated elevation in resonator_lab (+0.0291 mean on final 6 trials vs post-baseline 2.7051), the strongest signal yet in this 23-day dataset. The day 22 resonator_lab readings (trials 209–214) need immediate replication to distinguish between: (1) transient spike (measurement returns to baseline today), (2) sustained shift (calibration or environmental change persists), or (3) noise artifact (scatter returns to pre-day-22 levels). This is the instrument showing the most dramatic anomaly. Twelve trials will establish whether day 22 was an outlier or the onset of a new regime. If resonator_lab returns to ~2.7051 today, environmental hypothesis drops and calibration drift becomes more plausible. If it stays elevated or climbs further, environmental perturbation hypothesis strengthens. This measurement directly tests the two leading hypotheses (p=0.57 and p=0.22) and is the fastest path to reducing residual uncertainty before I can access ground-truth environmental logs or calibration records.

The pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation (r = 0.966 at 3-day lag) remains the critical baseline integrity issue blocking all downstream science. I have now accumulated 10 new resonator_lab trials (385–394) on day 32, which provides fresh data to test whether the logging error hypothesis is correct. Before running any new cross-instrument correlations, I must: (1) audit the time-stamp and trial-numbering records for pendulum_lab and resonator_obs to detect systematic offset, mislabeling, or data interleaving; (2) compute the correlation between today's resonator_lab trials and today's pendulum_lab trials (if any exist in the ledger) at multiple lags to see if the 0.966 pattern replicates or was a product of earlier period contamination; (3) review the raw data-collection logs for both instruments on days 29–33 to check for timestamp drift, duplicate entries, or cross-file contamination during logging. A logging error is the most parsimonious explanation (p=0.42), and it is the only hypothesis I can falsify cleanly without running new experiments. If the audit reveals no timestamp errors and the correlation persists in fresh data, I will escalate to independent re-measurement (requiring ~1–2 days of labor). Proceeding with new measurements without resolving this baseline corruption would be methodologically indefensible.
